prompt: Which three types of noncovalent interaction does the text describe?

choices.text: Dipole–dipole forces, dispersion forces, and hydrogen bonds
Covalent bonds, ionic bonds, and hydrogen bonds
choices.why: Covalent bonds are the interactions between atoms within a molecule; noncovalent interactions act between molecules.

choices.text: σ bonds, π bonds, and dispersion forces
choices.why: σ and π bonds are covalent bonds within molecules, not interactions between molecules.

choices.text: Resonance, dipole–dipole forces, and dispersion forces
choices.why: Resonance describes electron distribution within one molecule; it isn't a force between molecules.

explanation: Interactions between molecules, collectively called intermolecular forces, van der Waals forces, or noncovalent interactions, are of several types: dipole–dipole forces, dispersion forces, and hydrogen bonds.

choices.text: Electrostatic interactions among the dipoles of polar molecules
Temporary dipoles in nonpolar molecules
choices.why: Temporary dipoles cause dispersion forces, which act between all neighboring molecules.

choices.text: Sharing of electron pairs between molecules
choices.why: Sharing electron pairs makes covalent bonds; dipole–dipole forces are electrostatic attractions and repulsions.

choices.text: A hydrogen bonded to carbon
choices.why: Dipole–dipole forces don't need any particular hydrogen; any polar molecules have them.

explanation: Dipole–dipole forces occur between polar molecules as a result of electrostatic interactions among dipoles.

prompt: Dipole–dipole forces can be attractive or repulsive. Why does the attractive arrangement predominate?

choices.text: With unlike charges together, the arrangement is lower in energy
Polar molecules can only orient with unlike charges together
choices.why: Molecules can also orient with like charges together; those repel, as in Figure 2.12.1(b).

choices.text: With like charges together, the arrangement is lower in energy
choices.why: Like charges repel. The lower-energy, attractive geometry puts unlike charges together.

choices.text: Repulsive forces are always weaker than attractive ones
choices.why: The reason is energy: the attractive orientation is lower in energy, so it is favored.

explanation: Dipole–dipole forces are attractive when unlike charges are together and repulsive when like charges are together. The attractive geometry is lower in energy and therefore predominates (Figure 2.12.1).

prompt: Between which molecules do dispersion forces occur?

choices.text: Between all neighboring molecules, polar or nonpolar
Only between polar molecules
choices.why: Dispersion forces come from temporary dipoles, which form even in nonpolar molecules such as pentane.

choices.text: Only between molecules with O–H or N–H bonds
choices.why: That requirement describes hydrogen bonds. Dispersion forces need no special bonds.

choices.text: Only between ions
choices.why: Dispersion forces act between all neighboring molecules, including neutral, nonpolar ones.

explanation: Dispersion forces occur between all neighboring molecules. They arise because the electron distribution within molecules is constantly changing, so even nonpolar molecules form temporary dipoles.

choices.text: A temporary dipole in one molecule induces a temporarily opposite dipole in a neighbor
Permanent dipoles in polar molecules
choices.why: Permanent dipoles cause dipole–dipole forces. Dispersion forces come from fleeting, constantly changing dipoles.

choices.text: A hydrogen on O or N attracting a lone pair on another O or N
choices.why: That describes a hydrogen bond.

choices.text: Electron transfer between neighboring molecules
choices.why: No electrons move between molecules. Each molecule's own electrons shift momentarily to one side.

explanation: At any instant one side of a molecule may by chance have a slight excess of electrons, giving it a temporary dipole. That dipole causes a nearby molecule to adopt a temporarily opposite dipole, resulting in a tiny attraction (Figure 2.12.2).

prompt: Temporary molecular dipoles exist only fleetingly. Why do dispersion forces still matter?

choices.text: Their cumulative effect can hold molecules close enough together that a substance is a liquid or solid rather than a gas
Each one is stronger than a covalent bond
choices.why: Each attraction is tiny; it's their combined effect that matters.

choices.text: They make nonpolar molecules permanently polar
choices.why: The dipoles are temporary and constantly changing; on average the electron distribution stays uniform.

choices.text: They let nonpolar molecules dissolve in water
choices.why: Substances without groups that form hydrogen bonds, such as vegetable oil, don't dissolve in water.

explanation: Temporary molecular dipoles have only a fleeting existence and are constantly changing, but their cumulative effect is often strong enough to hold molecules close together so that a substance is a liquid or solid rather than a gas.

prompt: Pentane, C5H12, is nonpolar. What attractive force acts between its molecules (Figure 2.12.2)?

choices.text: Dispersion forces from temporary dipoles
Hydrogen bonds
choices.why: Pentane has only C–H bonds. Hydrogen bonds need a hydrogen on O or N.

choices.text: Dipole–dipole forces from permanent dipoles
choices.why: A nonpolar molecule has no permanent dipole; its dipoles are temporary.

choices.text: No attractive forces at all
choices.why: Dispersion forces act between all neighboring molecules, even nonpolar ones.

explanation: Attractive dispersion forces in nonpolar molecules such as pentane are caused by temporary dipoles (Figure 2.12.2).

choices.text: An attraction between a hydrogen bonded to O or N and an unshared electron pair on another O or N
A covalent bond between two hydrogen atoms
choices.why: That's the bond in H2. A hydrogen bond is a noncovalent attraction between molecules.

choices.text: An attraction between any hydrogen and any neighboring atom
choices.why: The hydrogen must be bonded to electronegative O or N so that it is strongly positively polarized.

choices.text: The bond between hydrogen and oxygen inside a water molecule
choices.why: The O–H bond within water is covalent. A hydrogen bond links that hydrogen to a lone pair on another molecule.

explanation: A hydrogen bond is an attractive interaction between a hydrogen atom bonded to an electronegative O or N atom and an unshared electron pair on another O or N atom.

prompt: In essence, what kind of interaction is a hydrogen bond?

choices.text: A very strong dipole–dipole interaction involving polarized O–H or N–H bonds
A dispersion force between temporary dipoles
choices.why: The polarized O–H and N–H bonds involved are permanent, not temporary dipoles.

choices.text: A weak covalent bond
choices.why: A hydrogen bond is a noncovalent interaction; no electron pair is shared.

choices.text: An ionic bond between H^+ and an anion
choices.why: The molecules stay neutral; the attraction is between a δ+ hydrogen and a lone pair.

explanation: In essence, a hydrogen bond is a very strong dipole–dipole interaction involving polarized O–H or N–H bonds.

prompt: Which of these substances forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules?

choices.text: Ammonia, NH3
Pentane, C5H12
choices.why: Pentane has only C–H bonds; its molecules attract one another through dispersion forces.

choices.text: Methane, CH4
choices.why: A hydrogen bonded to carbon isn't positively polarized enough; hydrogen bonds need an H on O or N.

choices.text: Vegetable oil
choices.why: Vegetable oil has no groups that form hydrogen bonds, which is why it doesn't dissolve in water.

explanation: Hydrogen bonds involve polarized O–H or N–H bonds. Electrostatic potential maps of water and ammonia show the positively polarized hydrogens (blue) and the negatively polarized oxygens and nitrogens (red).

prompt: What makes water a liquid rather than a gas at ordinary temperatures?

choices.text: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules
Covalent bonds between water molecules
choices.why: The covalent O–H bonds are inside each molecule; what holds the molecules together are noncovalent hydrogen bonds.

choices.text: Dispersion forces alone
choices.why: Dispersion forces act between all molecules, but the text credits hydrogen bonds for water being a liquid.

choices.text: Ionic bonds between H^+ and OH^−
choices.why: Water is made of neutral molecules; their polarized O–H bonds form hydrogen bonds.

explanation: Hydrogen bonding has enormous consequences for living organisms: hydrogen bonds cause water to be a liquid rather than a gas at ordinary temperatures.

prompt: Which is a role of hydrogen bonds in living organisms described in the text?

choices.text: They cause DNA strands to pair up and coil into the double helix
They join the atoms within each DNA strand
choices.why: The atoms within a strand are joined by covalent bonds; hydrogen bonds pair the two strands.

choices.text: They make vegetable oil dissolve in water
choices.why: Vegetable oil has no groups that form hydrogen bonds, so it doesn't dissolve in water.

choices.text: They break apart enzymes so they can act
choices.why: The reverse: hydrogen bonds hold enzymes in the shapes needed to catalyze reactions.

explanation: Hydrogen bonds cause water to be a liquid at ordinary temperatures, hold enzymes in the shapes necessary for catalyzing biological reactions, and cause strands of DNA to pair up and coil into the double helix that stores genetic information.

prompt: Why does table sugar dissolve in water?

choices.text: It has many –OH groups that can form hydrogen bonds with water, making it hydrophilic
It has no groups that form hydrogen bonds, making it hydrophobic
choices.why: That describes vegetable oil, which does not dissolve in water.

choices.text: It is held together only by dispersion forces
choices.why: Sugar's many –OH groups let it form hydrogen bonds; that's what lets it dissolve.

choices.text: It is nonpolar
choices.why: Sugar's –OH groups contain polarized O–H bonds; nonpolar substances such as oil don't dissolve in water.

explanation: Hydrophilic ("water-loving") substances, such as table sugar, often have a number of –OH groups in their structure so they can form hydrogen bonds and dissolve in water.

prompt: What does hydrophobic mean, as biochemists use the term?

choices.text: "Water-fearing": not strongly attracted to water
"Water-loving": attracted to water
choices.why: That is hydrophilic.

choices.text: Able to form many hydrogen bonds with water
choices.why: Forming hydrogen bonds with water makes a substance hydrophilic, like table sugar.

choices.text: Containing many –OH groups
choices.why: Many –OH groups make a substance hydrophilic; hydrophobic substances lack groups that form hydrogen bonds.

explanation: Hydrophobic, meaning "water-fearing," describes a substance that is not strongly attracted to water. Hydrophobic substances, such as vegetable oil, do not have groups that form hydrogen bonds and do not dissolve in water.

prompt: Vitamin A is fat-soluble, while vitamin C is water-soluble. How is vitamin A described?

choices.text: Hydrophobic
Hydrophilic
choices.why: Hydrophilic substances dissolve in water; that describes vitamin C. A fat-soluble substance is hydrophobic.

choices.text: Both hydrophilic and hydrophobic
choices.why: Of the two vitamins, one is hydrophilic and the other hydrophobic; vitamin A is the hydrophobic one.

choices.text: Able to form many hydrogen bonds with water
choices.why: Substances that form hydrogen bonds with water are hydrophilic and dissolve in water, like vitamin C. Fat-soluble vitamin A is not strongly attracted to water.

explanation: Of vitamins A and C, vitamin C is water-soluble (hydrophilic) and vitamin A is fat-soluble (hydrophobic) (Exercise 2.12.1). A fat-soluble substance is not strongly attracted to water.
